title: Good design hasn’t changed with AI — John Pham, SF Compute

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is primarily about product design, UX, trust, accessibility, and human-centered design principles for AI products. Design principles are cross-domain but demonstrated through SF Compute, a developer-facing GPU cloud platform. The talk covers design principles and their technical implementation during product development. Accessible to engineers with basic web development knowledge but includes technical implementation details like Core Web Vitals and SSR. Conference presentation recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. All claims are directly supported by excerpts from the transcript.

summary: John Pham's talk asserts that good design principles remain unchanged in the AI era. Design is not just pretty pixels or animations—it is owned by everyone involved in building a product and encompasses every user touchpoint including UIs, APIs, error messages, docs, emails, and social media. In the age of AI and vibe coding, feature parity is no longer a differentiator; the human experience of design is what sets products apart. Pham presents four pillars: Speed, Trust, Accessibility, and Delight. Speed means perceived performance—first paint under 300ms (below the ~400ms human perception threshold), 60fps+ interactions, minimal bundle sizes, and gamifiable metrics like LCP, INP, and CLS. Trust means setting expectations, preventing errors, providing affordances, and never lying to users—exemplified by clear onboarding step counts, progress indicators, honest sales-call framing, pre-selected calendar times in local time zones, sane form defaults, unit flexibility (days/hours/weeks), and prioritizing user savings over revenue. Accessibility means building for everyone including screen reader users, considering contrast and motion, respecting reduced-motion preferences, using semantic HTML with form labels, leveraging browser autocomplete attributes, and preventing layout shift. Delight is driven by care, user rewards, and storytelling—color psychology using blues and greens to slow perceived time, the peak-end bias ending onboarding with a San Francisco reveal, a live GPU habitat camera feed built with stacked divs and looping video, and a prediction cone for nested menus that maps user intent for supernatural-feeling navigation. As a case study, SF Compute's onboarding and GPU purchasing flows address legal compliance requirements through design techniques that reduce perceived friction while prioritizing user experience over short-term revenue.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: AI has not changed the core principles of good design; feature parity is no longer a differentiator in the vibe-coding era.
Design is owned by everyone building a product, not just people with designer titles—it covers every user touchpoint.
Speed: aim for first paint under 300ms, 60fps+, minimal bundle sizes, and prefer fast browser primitives (stack divs) over slow alternatives (shaders, canvas).
Trust: set expectations, prevent errors, never lie to users, forgive mistakes, provide sane defaults, allow unit flexibility, and prioritize user savings over revenue.
Accessibility: use browser autocomplete, semantic HTML, form labels, prevent layout shift, and respect reduced-motion preferences.
Progressive disclosure reduces cognitive load by breaking forms into smaller steps that feel easier than one giant form.
Delight comes from care, user rewards, and storytelling—color psychology, peak-end bias, live camera feeds, and prediction cones for menus.
Complex visual effects can be achieved with tiny assets and no third-party JavaScript—a fog animation used a single 14kb image.
Showing care for users (e.g., finding them better prices) can increase long-term revenue even when it reduces short-term revenue.
Prediction cones map user intent for nested menu navigation, making hover interactions feel supernatural instead of janky.

sections.title: Introduction: Design Principles Unchanged by AI
sections.summary: Pham introduces the talk's thesis: AI hasn't changed good design principles. Design is a human thing owned by everyone, not just designers. It encompasses every touchpoint—UIs, APIs, error messages, docs, emails, tweets—and affects how users feel. Feature parity is no longer a differentiator in the AI/vibe-coding era; design is.

sections.title: The Four Pillars: Speed, Trust, Accessibility, Delight
sections.summary: Pham outlines four principles. Speed (perceived time, feedback, jank) makes products feel fast. Trust (state, error prevention, affordances) means products never lie and forgive mistakes. Accessibility (screen readers, contrast, motion) ensures products work for everyone. Delight (care, user rewards, story) creates memorable, shareable experiences. He assigns homework: apply these to your current product.

sections.title: Case Study: SF Compute Speed and Fog Animation
sections.summary: SF Compute, a GPU cloud provider, must collect compliance info for US export laws, adding friction. Pham shows how speed mitigates this: first paint under 300ms, 60fps+, minimal bundle. The signature fog effect uses a single 14kb transparent image duplicated with varied offsets, opacities, and speeds to create depth and event-driven density—no third-party JavaScript needed.

sections.title: Trust: Expectation Setting in Onboarding
sections.summary: Trust is built through expectation setting: telling users onboarding takes three steps under a minute, disclosing extra steps for business accounts, showing progress to trigger the endowment effect, reframing onboarding calls as non-sales engineer conversations, pre-selecting calendar times, and using local time zones.

sections.title: Accessibility: Reduced Motion and Form Optimization
sections.summary: Pham pauses all animations when reduced motion preference is detected. Address forms use browser autocomplete attributes so users can fill entire forms with one button. Layout shift is prevented so buttons don't move before clicks. Progressive disclosure breaks onboarding into three steps to reduce cognitive load. Every input has form labels, semantic HTML is used, and screen reader testing is recommended.

sections.title: Delight: Color Psychology and Peak-End Bias
sections.summary: Pham explains how blues and greens are chosen to slow users' perception of time during onboarding. The onboarding ends by revealing a beautiful San Francisco scene, leveraging the peak-end psychological bias so users remember the ending and forget the hardship they went through.

sections.title: GPU Buying: Live Camera Feed and Habitat
sections.summary: The GPU buying page lets users pick GPU type, environment, count, and duration. A live camera feed into the GPU habitat shows buyers the exact GPUs they're purchasing as specs change. Implementation uses stacked divs (fast) rather than shaders/canvas (slow), a small looping video, and browser primitives with no third-party JavaScript. Panning works by translating video within a viewport; zoom zooms the video. Forms have sane defaults, error nudging, and unit flexibility (days/hours/weeks). A GPU-to-tensor-core loading state provides domain-relevant delight. The system sacrifices short-term revenue by finding users better prices on sale orders.

sections.title: Lightning Round: Banners and Prediction Cone
sections.summary: Pham warns that banners cause layout shift and should not render with shift. He demonstrates a nested menu with a prediction cone, built at Vercel, that maps user intent as they hover, eliminating the need for precise pointer movements and making navigation feel supernatural.

demonstrations: SF Compute onboarding flow showing fast page load from Google search to onboarding
Fog animation built from a single 14kb transparent image: duplicate, offset transforms, vary opacity and speed, control density via opacity and layer count
Onboarding expectation setting: 'three steps, under a minute', progress updates, additional step disclosure for business accounts
Onboarding call reframing: explicitly stated as not a sales call, engineers talk to users, referrals to competitors if not a fit
Pre-selected calendar time to reduce friction, with opt-in for manual selection
Local time zone display instead of UTC/EST confusion
Reduced motion accommodation pausing all animations when preference is set
Browser autocomplete attribute filling entire address forms with a single button
Progressive disclosure: onboarding split into three steps instead of one giant step to reduce cognitive load
Color psychology: blues and greens chosen to slow users' perception of time during onboarding
Peak-end bias: onboarding ends by revealing a beautiful San Francisco scene so users forget the hardship
GPU habitat live camera feed showing exact GPUs buyers are purchasing, updating as specs change
Camera feed implemented with stacked divs (fast) rather than shaders/canvas (slow), looping video with no continuous loop to avoid motion sickness
Camera panning implemented as translating a video within a viewport, zoom as zooming the video
Loading state styled as GPU-to-tensor-core transformation for domain-relevant delight
Revenue sacrifice: system finds users better prices on sale orders, making less money but saving users money

Animated looping fog background can cause motion sickness in some users
Some application parts require loading states despite the goal of zero loading states
Not maximizing short-term revenue by finding users better prices
